title: Ash at Misenum: The Last Dated Words of Pompeii and Herculaneum
subtitle: Vesuvius and the buried towns of the Bay of Naples, AD 26–79 (and the writers who looked back)
intro: There is no diary of the last days of Pompeii. Nobody in the buried towns kept one that survived, and the people who saw Vesuvius erupt in AD 79 left us, in all, one eyewitness account: two letters written by Pliny the Younger to the historian Tacitus about twenty-seven years afterwards. This chapter is therefore built differently from the others. It sets that single eyewitness beside the last dated words of the towns themselves — receipts, loan contracts, sworn oaths and court pledges on wax tablets, a charcoal scrawl and the election notices on the walls — and beside the later writers who shaped how the disaster was remembered.

The documents have a strange power precisely because they are not about the eruption. A banker in Pompeii pays the town for a tax contract; a woman collects her auction money; a grain dealer at Puteoli pledges his wheat and swears by the emperor's guardian spirit; a young woman in Herculaneum goes to law to prove she was born free. Each is dated to the day by Roman consuls, and each was preserved only because the mountain buried it. They are the 'ordinary days' this book always needs — here, ordinary decades.

The towns had been warned, though no one read the warning. A great earthquake around 5 February 62 (or 63 — the sources disagree) wrecked Pompeii and damaged Herculaneum; Seneca wrote a treatise on earthquakes in response, and the household of the banker Caecilius Iucundus carved the falling temple and gate onto its family shrine. Seventeen years of rebuilding followed; the election notices show a working town still arguing about its aediles.

Then comes the eruption itself, seen through Pliny: his uncle the admiral sailing into the ash cloud and dying on the beach at Stabiae; the seventeen-year-old reading Livy as the house shakes, then fleeing Misenum with his mother into a darkness he likens to a sealed room with the lamp put out. Every scene of the elder Pliny is second-hand, reported by the nephew, and flagged as such. Cassius Dio, writing a century and a half later, adds giants on the mountain and a crowd caught in the theatre; Suetonius records the emperor Titus's relief commissioners. The library at the Villa of the Papyri stands for what was lost: books, not records.

Even the date is contested. Pliny's manuscripts overwhelmingly give 24 August, but autumn fruit, heavy clothing and a charcoal note dated 17 October — found in 2018 in a house in Regio V — persuaded many that the eruption came on or around 24 October. The latest manuscript and experimental work has pushed back toward August. The calendar note sets out the case; the timeline places the eruption at Pliny's date and shows the October note where it falls, so readers can see both.

Form tags are honest throughout: these are letters, documents, inscriptions, histories and books, not diaries. The forms are the point — an empire whose ordinary people left their dates on wax, wall and receipt, and whose one eyewitness wrote as a literary man looking back.
calendar_note: All dates are in the Julian calendar, which was in actual use in AD 79 (no proleptic conversion is needed); date_iso uses year '0079'. Romans counted backwards inclusively from fixed points in the month — the Kalends (1st), Nones (5th or 7th) and Ides (13th or 15th) — and named years by the two consuls in Rome (and in Pompeii also by local duumvirs). So Pliny's 'ninth day before the Kalends of September' is 24 August, and the Regio V charcoal note's 'sixteenth day before the Kalends of November' is 17 October. THE DATE DEBATE: the medieval manuscripts of Pliny's Letter 6.16 overwhelmingly read 24 August, though some have gaps or garbled month abbreviations (n/v confusions such as 'nov') that later scholars read as November or, by an emendation proposed in the early twentieth century, 24 October. The case for autumn rests on Cassius Dio's phrase usually rendered 'at the beginning of autumn' or 'end of summer' (in Roman farming calendars autumn began around 8 August), on autumn fruits such as pomegranates and chestnuts found in the ruins, on braziers and heavy woollen clothing, on a coin of Titus once read with an acclamation datable after early September (the reading is now doubted), and on the charcoal note of 17 October. Against it: P. Foss's 2022 collation found 24 August in about 95% of relevant manuscripts; a 2024 experiment showed charcoal writing can stay legible outdoors for ten months, so the note may date from October 78; a Hermann's tortoise found with an unlaid egg points to early summer; and a Pompeii Park study in December 2024 found no documentary basis for 24 October. This chapter therefore places the eruption on 24–25 August by Pliny's text and the charcoal note at 17 October, with confidence marked approx. Beware of yearless dates: another Pompeii graffito records that on 17 October a female called Puteolana gave birth to a litter of five — the same day-month, no year, and no bearing on the eruption. The Campanian earthquake is placed on 5 February 62 by convention; Seneca's own consular date gives 63, and some scholars think there were two quakes.

eyes.name: Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus (Pliny the Younger)
eyes.role: Seventeen years old in 79 (he says he was in his eighteenth year); nephew and adopted heir of the fleet commander; later a senator, consul (100) and governor of Bithynia
eyes.side: Roman; household of the prefect of the Misenum fleet
eyes.where: The family house at Misenum, at the north-west tip of the Bay of Naples, about 30 km across the water from Vesuvius
eyes.form: dated letters (memoir written later: two letters composed c. AD 106–107, about 27 years after the event)
eyes.authenticity: Letters 6.16 and 6.20, written at the request of the historian Tacitus and published in Book 6 of Pliny's collected letters, usually dated c. 106–107. Not a diary: polished literary prose written a quarter-century later, by a man who says himself that he is writing a letter, not history. Survives in medieval manuscripts (oldest 9th century); the day of the eruption is given as the ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August) in the great majority of manuscripts, though some have gaps or garbled month names, which fuels the date debate. English: Melmoth's translation revised by Bosanquet (letters LXV–LXVI in the Project Gutenberg edition).
eyes.bio: The only eyewitness account of the eruption to survive from antiquity. Pliny stayed home to study while his uncle sailed off, then fled Misenum with his mother through falling ash and darkness the next morning. He wrote it up decades later, partly to secure his uncle's heroic memory in Tacitus's Histories, and partly — he admits — because Tacitus asked what he himself had been through. His second letter is careful to say he lived through only the fringe of the disaster.

sources.title: Letters of Pliny (Melmoth, rev. Bosanquet) — Project Gutenberg #2811
Same, HTML edition

eyes.name: Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder)
eyes.role: Prefect commanding the imperial fleet at Misenum, aged 56; equestrian official and author of the encyclopaedic Natural History (dedicated to Titus in 77)
eyes.where: Sailed from Misenum across the bay toward the coast below Vesuvius, then to Stabiae, where he died on the shore

waypoints.label: Misenum: sees the cloud, launches the fleet
Coast below Vesuvius: ash and shoals block landing
Stabiae: house of Pomponianus; dies on the shore

eyes.vantage_label: principal actor, seen only through his nephew
eyes.form: seen through another's letter (no writing of his own survives about the eruption)
eyes.authenticity: Everything here comes from his nephew's Letter 6.16, written c. 106–107 and openly designed to honour him; the details of his last night at Stabiae must have come from survivors of his party, whom the nephew does not name. Later traditions (e.g. a note in Suetonius's lost life of Pliny, preserved in fragments) offered other versions of his death, including that he asked a slave to kill him; Pliny's nephew gives the natural-death version. Treat the scenes as a family account, not a log.
eyes.bio: A tireless naturalist and naval commander, he first rowed toward the eruption out of scientific curiosity and then turned it into a rescue. His last day — the cloud like an umbrella pine, the note from a frightened friend, a bath and a dinner at Stabiae, sleep amid falling pumice, death on the beach — is the most famous scene in Roman disaster writing. He is here as a deliberately flagged 'second-hand eye'.

sources.title: Pliny the Younger, Letter 6.16 (Melmoth/Bosanquet, Gutenberg #2811)

eyes.name: Lucius Caecilius Iucundus and his household archive
eyes.life: fl. c. AD 52–62; probably dead before 79
eyes.role: Pompeian auctioneer-banker (argentarius) and son of a freedman; arranged auctions for clients, advanced credit to buyers and leased public revenues from the town, taking a small commission
eyes.where: House of Caecilius Iucundus (V.1.26), Via del Vesuvio, Pompeii
eyes.vantage_label: inside the city: dated receipts, then the earthquake
eyes.form: administrative documents (dated wax-tablet receipts) and a carved relief
eyes.authenticity: 153–154 waxed wooden tablets found in 1875 in an upper part of the house, published in CIL IV supplement (Zangemeister). Two date from AD 15 and 27 and probably belong to his father Felix; the rest run from the 50s to AD 62, none later. The receipts are dated by Roman consuls and by Pompeian duumvirs, so most have exact days. The two marble lararium reliefs of the earthquake are not dated documents; one was stolen in 1975 and recovered in 2023.
eyes.bio: Not a diarist but a man whose business forced him to date everything. His receipts — a widow's auction money, a town slave collecting pasture rent — are the nearest thing to an ordinary Pompeian's daybook, and they fall silent in early 62, close to the great earthquake. His household then carved the quake into the family shrine: the town's only contemporary picture of a disaster, made seventeen years before the larger one.

sources.title: Cambridge Latin Course: Lucius Caecilius Iucundus
Pompeii Archaeological Park: House of Caecilius Iucundus
Fordham Ancient History Sourcebook: Pompeii inscriptions (receipts nos. 32–33)

eyes.name: The Sulpicii of Puteoli (Murecine archive)
eyes.life: Archive AD 26–61; C. Sulpicius Faustus, his freedman C. Sulpicius Cinnamus and C. Sulpicius Onirus
eyes.role: A family firm of freedman moneylenders and financial agents at Puteoli, the great grain port of Rome on the Bay of Naples
eyes.side: Puteoli commercial community (freedmen, merchants, imperial slaves)
eyes.where: Business at Puteoli; the archive was buried in a building at Murecine, about 600 m south of Pompeii

waypoints.label: Puteoli: deals made and documents written
Murecine near Pompeii: archive buried in 79

eyes.vantage_label: business archive across the bay, buried by the eruption
eyes.form: administrative documents (dated wax-tablet contracts, receipts, oaths)
eyes.authenticity: Found in a basket in 1959 during road-building at Murecine; about 127 tablets with more than 120 texts, dated AD 26–61 (TPSulp, ed. G. Camodeca, 1999). Many tablets deteriorated after excavation; early photographs are the best record. Why a Puteoli archive ended up near Pompeii is unknown. They end eighteen years before the eruption.
eyes.bio: The Sulpicii lent money against grain stored in warehouses and witnessed the oaths of debtors who swore by the reigning emperor's guardian spirit. Their tablets show the bay as a working economy of freedmen, imperial slaves and Alexandrian grain — the world the eruption buried — and they preserve something rare: a debtor's own handwriting, spelling mistakes and all.

sources.title: Judaism and Rome: An oath sworn to Jupiter (TPSulp 68)
Villa at Murecine (pompeii.pictures)
sources.url: https://pompeii.pictures/VF/Villa_050 Scafati Contrada Murecine, Fondo Cascone p1.htm

eyes.name: The Herculaneum tablets of Petronia Iusta's case
eyes.life: Case documents AD 74–75 (Petronia Iusta, her mother Petronia Vitalis, her patroness Calatoria Themis)
eyes.role: A young woman suing to prove she was born free, after her mother's manumission, against her mother's former owner who claimed her as a freedwoman
eyes.side: Herculaneum townspeople: freedwomen, freedmen and witnesses
eyes.where: House of the Bicentenary, Insula V, Herculaneum
eyes.vantage_label: inside the buried town: dated court papers
eyes.form: administrative documents (dated legal tablets: bail pledges and sworn testimony)
eyes.authenticity: Eighteen wax-covered wooden tablets found in a chest in 1938 in the House of the Bicentenary and published by Arangio-Ruiz and Pugliese Carratelli; re-edited by G. Camodeca. They include three vadimonia (pledges to appear in court, two dated 7 September 74 and 12 March 75) and seven testimonia. The outcome of the case is unknown; a firm internal chronology cannot be established.
eyes.bio: The best-documented private lawsuit from the buried towns, and one of the latest dated records from them: four or five years before the eruption, neighbours of a Herculaneum family swore oaths by the guardian spirit of Vespasian about who had been freed, and when. It is the voice of former slaves arguing about freedom in the very house that the ash sealed.

sources.title: Judaism and Rome: An oath sworn in Herculaneum by the genius of Vespasian
University of Aberdeen: The Case of Petronia Iusta

eyes.name: Unknown writer of the charcoal inscription (House with the Garden, Regio V)
eyes.role: Anonymous person — perhaps a worker or member of a household under renovation — who scrawled a dated note in charcoal on a wall
eyes.where: House with the Garden (Casa del Giardino), Regio V, Pompeii
eyes.vantage_label: inside the city: a scrawl with a day but no year
eyes.authenticity: Found during the Regio V excavations and announced in October 2018. Reads the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November (17 October) with no year; the rest is read by G. Ammannati as people taking something into an oil store. Excavators judged an AD 79 date very probable because charcoal is fragile; a 2024 experiment found charcoal writing survived ten months outdoors, and the room belonged to post-earthquake repairs, so 17 October 78 remains possible.
eyes.bio: A mundane jotting that turned into evidence in the eruption's longest-running dispute. If it was written in October 79, the town was still alive a week before an October eruption and Pliny's August date is wrong; if in 78, it is simply a last-year note. Either way it is a voice from a house where victims later took shelter.

sources.title: Pompeii Archaeological Park: Inscription discovered in Regio V
CNN (2018): inscription suggests later eruption date
nunc.ch: August 24 or October 24? The debate

eyes.name: Pompeii's election painters and their sponsors (programmata)
eyes.life: Notices of the town's last campaigns, 70s AD
eyes.role: Professional sign-painters who brushed red and black election notices on house fronts for candidates, on behalf of neighbours, trades and associations
eyes.side: Pompeii citizens: fullers, dyers, fruit-sellers, Isis worshippers, neighbours
eyes.form: inscriptions (painted public notices; not individually dated)
eyes.authenticity: Some 2,500+ electoral notices survive (CIL IV). They carry no dates; years are inferred by modern scholars from candidates' careers and from which notices were freshest when the town was buried. Assigning particular names (e.g. Cn. Helvius Sabinus) to the final campaign of 79 is scholarly reconstruction, not a stated date.
eyes.bio: The walls show a town still busy with local politics after the earthquake: dyers backing one aedile, the worshippers of Isis another, and joke-endorsements from 'late drinkers' and 'sneak thieves' that were probably rivals' mockery. They give the crowd's voice that no diary preserves.

sources.title: Fordham Sourcebook: Pompeii inscriptions (electoral notices)
World History Encyclopedia: Pompeii graffiti, signs and electoral notices
MANN / Google Arts & Culture: Elections in Pompeii

eyes.name: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
eyes.role: Stoic philosopher, dramatist and former adviser to Nero, in semi-retirement; writing his Natural Questions
eyes.where: Rome and his Italian villas, writing about Campania (a region he knew well)
eyes.vantage_label: in Italy, writing on the quake soon after
eyes.form: treatise (natural philosophy, written within a year or two of the event)
eyes.authenticity: Natural Questions book 6 opens with the Campanian earthquake, dating it to the Nones of February in the consulship of Regulus and Verginius — AD 63 — while Tacitus (Annals 15.22) puts a Pompeii earthquake in 62. Editors often delete the consular phrase as a gloss; others (e.g. E. Henry) argue there were two quakes. Not a diary, but the only near-contemporary narrative of the 62/63 disaster.
eyes.bio: Seneca wrote his treatise on earthquakes because the Campanian quake had just terrified Italy. He reports damage at Pompeii, Herculaneum and Nuceria, a flock of hundreds of sheep killed, a statue split, and people driven out of their minds — then turns to the philosopher's consolation: no place is safe, so fear nothing. He did not live to see Vesuvius erupt.

sources.title: Fear and Healing: Seneca, Caecilius Iucundus and the Campanian Earthquake of 62/63 CE (Greece & Rome)
E. Henry, The date of the Campanian earthquake: AD 62 or 63, or both? (review)

eyes.name: Lucius Cassius Dio
eyes.role: Greek-speaking Roman senator from Nicaea, twice consul; historian of Rome writing about 150 years after the eruption
eyes.where: Writing in Rome and Italy in the early third century
eyes.vantage_label: a century and a half later
eyes.authenticity: Roman History 66.21–24, preserved only in the Byzantine epitome of Xiphilinus, so Dio's wording is abridged. Places the eruption 'at the turn of autumn' or 'end of summer' — translators differ — which is cited in the date debate. Mixes eyewitness-sounding detail with legend (apparitions of giants).
eyes.bio: Dio offers the ancient world's second full narrative, and a completely different texture from Pliny's: giants seen walking on the mountain, an audience caught in the theatre at Pompeii, ash reaching Africa, Syria and Egypt and darkening Rome, and a plague afterwards. Valuable for how the disaster was remembered; unreliable as a record.

sources.title: Cassius Dio, Roman History book 66 (Cary, Loeb) — LacusCurtius

eyes.name: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus
eyes.role: Imperial biographer and secretary; a small child in 79; friend and protégé of Pliny the Younger
eyes.where: Rome, writing the Lives of the Caesars c. AD 120
eyes.authenticity: Life of Titus 8.3–4. Written about forty years after the event from palace records and memory; gives no date, but lists the eruption among the disasters of Titus's short reign. Reliable on administrative measures.
eyes.bio: Suetonius shows the view from the palace: not ash and darkness but relief policy — commissioners chosen by lot from former consuls to restore Campania, and the property of victims who died without heirs turned over to rebuilding the towns. Titus's reign became, in his telling, a test of an emperor's fatherly care.

sources.title: Suetonius, Life of Titus 8 (Lexundria)

eyes.name: The library of the Villa of the Papyri (Philodemus and others)
eyes.life: Books written mostly 1st century BC; buried AD 79
eyes.role: A private library of Greek philosophy, chiefly works of the Epicurean Philodemus of Gadara, in a seaside villa probably owned by the family of L. Calpurnius Piso
eyes.where: Villa of the Papyri, just outside Herculaneum
eyes.vantage_label: buried in the first surge: books, not records
eyes.form: books (literary scrolls — not dated records or diaries)
eyes.authenticity: About 1,800 carbonised papyrus fragments, perhaps 800 rolls, were excavated in 1752–54. They are copies of philosophical works, not personal or dated documents, and say nothing about the eruption. Since 2023 non-invasive scanning (the Vesuvius Challenge) has begun reading unopened rolls.
eyes.bio: Included as a deliberate contrast: the only library to survive from the classical world, sealed by the same pyroclastic flows that killed the people of Herculaneum. It records what an educated household was reading — Epicurean arguments about pleasure, death and the gods — not what anyone saw on the last day.

sources.title: Oxford: Herculaneum papyri

entries.headline: A Puteoli money firm starts its paper trail
entries.digest: The oldest tablets of the Sulpicii archive belong to the reign of Tiberius, when C. Sulpicius Faustus was lending money in Puteoli. The archive will run for some 35 years, passing from Faustus to his freedman Cinnamus and later to Onirus. Its tablets are dated by Roman consuls and day, like any formal contract.
entries.source_note: Archive date range AD 26–61 per Judaism and Rome database commentary on TPSulp (Camodeca ed.).

entries.headline: Grain in the warehouse pledged for a 10,000-sesterce loan
entries.digest: C. Novius Eunus, a grain dealer, borrows 10,000 sesterces; Faustus witnesses the deal. As security Eunus pledges wheat and other foodstuffs stored in the horrea Bassiana, a warehouse in Puteoli. It is a snapshot of the grain trade that fed Rome passing through the bay.
entries.source_note: TPSulp 51, summarised in the Judaism and Rome commentary on TPSulp 68.

entries.headline: A second loan two weeks later
entries.digest: Eunus comes back for 3,000 sesterces more, bringing his debt to 13,000. The tablets record the extra sum on the same security. The pace — two loans in a fortnight — suggests a merchant juggling cargoes and cash in the busy summer shipping season.
entries.source_note: TPSulp 52, per Judaism and Rome commentary.

entries.date_display: 15 September AD 39 (consuls Cn. Domitius Afer and A. Didius Gallus)
entries.headline: A debtor swears by Jupiter and Caligula's genius
entries.digest: Eunus acknowledges a remaining debt of 1,250 sesterces to the imperial slave Hesychus, payable by 1 November, with a penalty of 20 sesterces a day for lateness. He swears by Jupiter Best and Greatest, by the deified Augustus and by the guardian spirit of the emperor Gaius. The inner text is in Eunus's own hand, full of spelling mistakes; the outer copy was written by a scribe.
entries.source_note: TPSulp 68 (Judaism and Rome, record 203).

entries.headline: The banker pays the town for a tax contract
entries.digest: A receipt records Iucundus paying the town of Pompeii for a contract to collect a public revenue. Sixteen of his tablets are receipts of this kind, showing a private businessman farming the colony's income. Most of the rest are auction settlements for private clients.
entries.source_note: Cambridge Latin Course weblink and Wikipedia summary of the Iucundus tablets.

entries.date_display: 12 December AD 56 (consuls L. Duvius and P. Clodius)
entries.headline: A woman collects her auction money: 11,039 sesterces
entries.digest: Umbricia Ianuaria acknowledges receiving 11,039 sesterces from Iucundus — the proceeds of an auction he ran for her, after his commission was taken. The witnesses' names are listed in order of social rank. It is one of the few documents in which a Pompeian woman appears handling her own substantial money.
entries.source_note: Fordham Sourcebook, Pompeii inscriptions no. 32; Cambridge SCP weblink.

entries.date_display: 18 June AD 59 (consuls Cn. Fonteius and C. Vipstanus; duumvirs L. Veranius Hypsaeus and L. Albucius Iustus)
entries.headline: A town slave collects the rent for public pasture
entries.digest: Privatus, a slave owned by the colony of Pompeii, acknowledges payments from Iucundus for the lease of the town's public pastures, including a sum received on 6 June. The receipt is double-dated, by Rome's consuls and by Pompeii's own duumvirs. It is ordinary municipal bookkeeping, three years before the ground shook.
entries.source_note: Fordham Sourcebook, Pompeii inscriptions no. 33.

entries.headline: The Sulpicii tablets fall silent
entries.digest: The latest dated texts in the archive belong to AD 61, under Nero. Nothing explains why the firm's papers were later kept in a basket in a building at Murecine, outside Pompeii, where the eruption buried them eighteen years afterwards. They were found only in 1959, during roadworks.
entries.source_note: Archive date range and 1959 discovery per Judaism and Rome database.

entries.date_display: After the earthquake of AD 62/63 (relief undated)
entries.place: Pompeii, household shrine in the atrium
entries.headline: The household carves the earthquake into its shrine
entries.digest: Two marble reliefs on the household shrine show the quake: one the Temple of Jupiter in the forum tilting, the other the collapsing Vesuvius Gate beside the water tower, with a donkey cart. They are the only picture of the disaster made by Pompeians themselves, probably as thanks for survival. One was stolen in 1975 and found again in Belgium in 2023.
entries.source_note: Pompeii Archaeological Park page on the house; Museo Galileo description of the cast; relief undated, made between 62 and 79.

entries.headline: The receipts stop, days before the earthquake
entries.digest: Iucundus's dated records end in the weeks before the earthquake conventionally dated 5 February 62; none is later. His name does not appear in any known inscription of the 70s. Scholars infer he may have died in or soon after the quake; the archive itself was simply left in the house until the eruption sealed it.
entries.source_note: Cambridge SCP weblink (records stop shortly before February 62); exact last day not checked against CIL.

entries.date_display: Nones (5th) of February — Seneca names the consuls of AD 63; Tacitus puts the quake in AD 62
entries.headline: Campania shakes: Pompeii falls, Herculaneum partly ruined
entries.digest: Seneca reports that Pompeii, a busy Campanian town, had collapsed in a great earthquake, Herculaneum was partly destroyed, and Nuceria damaged. He notes it struck in winter, a season his forebears thought safe from quakes. Damage stretched to Naples.
entries.source_note: Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1.1–2; year disputed (AD 62 vs 63) per Henry 1984 and Greece & Rome article 'Fear and Healing'.

entries.headline: Six hundred sheep dead and minds unhinged: a philosopher on fear
entries.digest: Seneca collects strange aftereffects — a flock of hundreds of sheep killed, a statue split, people wandering out of their wits — and builds a treatise on why the earth shakes. His real aim is consolation: since no place is beyond danger, the only refuge is not to fear death. Campanians, he notes, were leaving the region.
entries.source_note: Seneca NQ 6.1, 6.27; summary via 'Fear and Healing' (Greece & Rome).

entries.headline: An illiterate witness swears by Vespasian's genius
entries.digest: Marcus Calatorius Marullus, who could not write, had a scribe set down his sworn statement that Calatoria Themis had freed the girl along with him — testimony on the patroness's side. He swore by the guardian spirit of the emperor Vespasian and his children. Five other sworn statements on the tablets support Iusta's claim to free birth, including neighbours recalling that the late co-patron Stephanus had only one woman, Vitalis, to free.
entries.source_note: Judaism and Rome record 192 (tablets 2–3; TH 16–20 testimonia).

entries.headline: A bail pledge: Petronia Iusta's case goes to the praetor
entries.digest: A vadimonium records a promise to appear before the praetor's court in Rome over Petronia Iusta's status. She claimed she was born after her mother Petronia Vitalis was freed, which would make her freeborn; her mother's former mistress, Calatoria Themis, said she was born a slave and so was a freedwoman owing duties to her patron.
entries.source_note: TH 14, per Judaism and Rome database (record 192) commentary.

entries.headline: Another court date set, four years before the end
entries.digest: A second dated bail pledge fixes another appearance in the case. The verdict is not preserved: the tablets were left in a chest in the House of the Bicentenary, where the eruption sealed them. They are among the latest dated private documents from the buried towns.
entries.source_note: TH 15, per Judaism and Rome database commentary.

entries.date_display: Spring AD 79? (undated; notices of the last campaigns)
entries.headline: Isis worshippers, dyers and 'late drinkers' endorse candidates
entries.digest: Freshly painted notices urge votes for aedile candidates such as Cn. Helvius Sabinus — backed by the worshippers of Isis — and Marcus Epidius Sabinus, backed by the residents of a suburb. Others push Vatia in the name of 'late drinkers', 'late risers' and 'sneak thieves', almost certainly mockery by opponents. Which of these were still current in 79 is a scholarly inference, not a dated fact.
entries.source_note: Fordham Sourcebook electoral notices nos. 5–16; World History Encyclopedia article; year of campaign inferred, not stated.

entries.date_display: AD 79–80 (no date given; written c. AD 120)
entries.headline: Commissioners by lot and the property of the heirless dead
entries.digest: Suetonius lists the eruption among the calamities of Titus's reign, with a three-day fire in Rome and a severe plague. Titus showed, he says, the concern of a parent: he chose commissioners by lot from former consuls to restore Campania, and gave the goods of those killed by Vesuvius who left no heirs to rebuild the stricken towns. Suetonius was a boy of about ten at the time.
entries.source_note: Suetonius, Titus 8.3–4 (Lexundria).

entries.headline: Trades and neighbours keep campaigning on the rebuilt town
entries.digest: The election notices on rebuilt walls show the town still had a functioning council and annual elections after the earthquake. Fullers, fruit-sellers and ball-players lend their names to candidates; neighbours sign together. Some candidates in this crop — such as Lucius Ceius Secundus — were backed by members of the Iucundus family.
entries.source_note: MANN/Google Arts & Culture 'Elections in Pompeii'; Iucundus son's graffito per Wikipedia article on Iucundus; month is illustrative, not dated.

entries.date_display: Ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August), about the seventh hour — early afternoon (manuscript date; see calendar note)
entries.headline: A cloud shaped like an umbrella pine
entries.digest: After sunbathing, a cold bath and a light lunch, the admiral is working when his sister points out a cloud of unusual size rising from a mountain across the bay — no one yet knew which. It shoots up on a tall trunk and spreads at the top like the crown of an umbrella pine, sometimes white, sometimes dirty with earth and ash. He orders a light galley made ready to go and look.
entries.source_note: Pliny, Letter 6.16.4–7 (Gutenberg #2811, Letter LXV); written c. 106.

entries.place: Bay of Naples, toward the coast below Vesuvius
entries.headline: Rectina's plea turns a science trip into a rescue
entries.digest: As he leaves, a message comes from Rectina, wife of Tascius, whose villa lay at the foot of the mountain with escape possible only by sea; she begs him to save her. He launches the big quadriremes instead and steers straight toward danger, dictating observations as he goes. Ash grows hotter and thicker, pumice and blackened stones fall, and a sudden shoal and rockfalls block the shore.

entries.headline: Fortune favours the brave: on to Stabiae
entries.digest: When his helmsman urges retreat he refuses and runs with the wind to Stabiae, where his friend Pomponianus has loaded a ship but cannot sail against the wind. To calm him, the admiral bathes, dines cheerfully and goes to sleep — his heavy breathing heard at the door — while flames glow on the mountain and he tells everyone they are only abandoned farm fires. The courtyard meanwhile fills with ash and pumice until his door is nearly blocked.
entries.source_note: Letter 6.16.11–13; the motto is reported as his words to the helmsman.

entries.headline: The seventeen-year-old chooses his books
entries.digest: Offered a place on his uncle's galley, Pliny replies that he would rather study — and, he adds, his uncle had happened to set him some writing. After the boats leave he spends the rest of the day at his books, then bathes, dines and sleeps fitfully. For several days there had been tremors, which no one thought alarming because they were common in Campania.
entries.source_note: Letter 6.16.7 and 6.20.1–3 (Gutenberg #2811, Letters LXV–LXVI).

entries.headline: Reading Livy while the house shakes
entries.digest: That night the shocks become so violent that things seem not just to move but to be overturned. His mother bursts into his room; they sit in the small courtyard between house and sea, and he — unsure whether it is courage or foolishness — calls for a volume of Livy and goes on making notes. A friend of his uncle, just arrived from Spain, scolds the mother's patience and the son's complacency.
entries.source_note: Letter 6.20.4–5.

entries.date_display: Late summer / autumn AD 79 (Dio gives no day; written c. AD 220–230)
entries.place: Retold in Rome a century and a half later
entries.headline: Giants on the mountain and a town caught in its theatre
entries.digest: Dio tells of huge figures like the Giants of myth seen on the mountain and in the air before the outbreak, of droughts and earthquakes, then a crash, flying stones and a darkness that hid the sun. People thought the Giants were rising again or that the world was ending. He says ash buried Herculaneum and Pompeii, the latter while its people sat in the theatre — a detail with no archaeological support.
entries.source_note: Cassius Dio 66.21–23 (Xiphilinus epitome), LacusCurtius (Cary).

entries.date_display: 24 August AD 79 (by Pliny's date; burial date shared with Herculaneum)
entries.headline: A library of philosophy buried in its rooms
entries.digest: Hundreds of rolls of Greek philosophy, mostly by the Epicurean Philodemus — on music, rhetoric, death, the gods and Plato's school — are entombed and carbonised by the volcanic flows that overwhelmed Herculaneum. They contain no record of the day itself. Excavated in 1752–54, they are now being read without unrolling by X-ray scanning and machine learning.
entries.source_note: Oxford Herculaneum papyri page; not a dated record — date is that of burial.

entries.headline: Pillows on their heads, they walk to the sea
entries.digest: Woken and the house shaking, the party debates whether to stay under roofs or risk the falling stones, and chooses the open, tying pillows on their heads with cloths. Elsewhere it is day, but here a night darker than any night, lit by torches. At the shore the sea is still too rough; he lies on a spread sail, asks twice for cold water, then flames and a smell of sulphur send the others running. Supported by two slaves he stands up and collapses — his nephew believes the dense fumes choked a windpipe that was often weak.

entries.headline: The sea sucked back; a black cloud over the bay
entries.digest: In faint, sickly daylight they leave town with a panicking crowd that presses after them. Carts set on level ground roll back and forth even when wedged with stones; the sea seems to be drawn back, leaving sea creatures stranded. Across the bay a dreadful black cloud, split by twisting fire like long lightning, comes down to the water and hides Capri and the headland of Misenum.

entries.headline: Darkness like a shut room, and a mother's plea
entries.digest: His mother begs him to save himself and leave her, old and slow; he refuses and drags her on. Ash begins to fall and a darkness descends, not like a moonless night but like a sealed room with the lamp put out. They hear women wailing, children crying, men shouting; some pray for death out of fear of death, many think the gods are gone and the world's last night has come, and some spread false rumours that Misenum has fallen. He shakes the ash off repeatedly to avoid being buried and crushed.

entries.headline: Thin daylight, a world under snow, and waiting
entries.digest: At last the darkness thins like smoke, real daylight returns and even a pale sun, and everything they see is changed, buried deep in ash as if under snow. They go back to Misenum, refresh themselves and spend an anxious night between hope and fear; the tremors continue and some people make crazed prophecies. They refuse to leave until they have news of his uncle.

entries.date_display: Third day after he was last seen (26 August by the traditional date)
entries.headline: His body is found, looking asleep
entries.digest: When daylight returns, the third day from the one he was last seen, his body is found intact and uninjured, still dressed as he had been. In his nephew's words it looked more like a man asleep than dead. The nephew ends the letter abruptly, saying the rest is not for history.

entries.headline: Ash reaches Rome and Egypt; a plague follows
entries.digest: Dio claims so much ash was carried that it reached Africa, Syria and Egypt, and darkened Rome, where people panicked for days not knowing what had happened. He adds that the dust did no immediate harm in the capital but later brought a terrible pestilence. The distances are likely exaggerated; Rome's later epidemic is attested elsewhere but its link to the ash is Dio's own idea.
entries.source_note: Cassius Dio 66.23, LacusCurtius.

entries.date_display: 16th day before the Kalends of November = 17 October (year not written: AD 79 or earlier)
entries.place: House with the Garden, Regio V, Pompeii
entries.headline: A charcoal note: 'they took' something to the oil store
entries.digest: On a wall of a house under refurbishment someone wrote in charcoal the date 17 October and a note read as people taking supplies into the oil pantry — perhaps a record of over-eating or of stock being moved. If written in 79, it means the house was in ordinary use one week before an October eruption. Because no year is given, it could equally be from 78.
entries.source_note: Pompeii Archaeological Park press page; CNN 2018; nunc.ch summary of the 2024 charcoal-durability experiment.

entries.headline: Rome burns while Titus is in Campania
entries.digest: The next year a great fire raged in Rome for days while the emperor was away in Campania seeing to the disaster. Titus sent two former consuls to oversee Campania's recovery, gave money, and assigned the estates of those who died without heirs to the survivors. He refused gifts from cities and private people and paid for repairs from his own funds.
entries.source_note: Cassius Dio 66.24, LacusCurtius.

entries.headline: Writing it up for Tacitus, 27 years on
entries.digest: Tacitus, gathering material for his Histories, asks how Pliny's uncle died; Pliny answers in a letter promising that the death will be made immortal by Tacitus's work. A second letter answers Tacitus's follow-up about Pliny's own experience. He frames both as raw material, not history — yet they are crafted literary prose, written with hindsight and a family reputation at stake.
entries.source_note: Letters 6.16.1–3, 6.16.22, 6.20.1, 6.20.20; date of Book 6 is conventional scholarly dating.

convergences.label: The Campanian earthquake
convergences.note: Seneca, writing in Rome, turns the quake into a lesson against fear; in Pompeii the banker's receipts have stopped just before it, and his household carves the falling temple and gate onto its shrine. The philosopher's abstraction and the family's thank-offering for survival describe the same rubble.

convergences.label: The eruption begins (Pliny's date)
convergences.note: At Misenum the uncle sails toward the cloud while the nephew stays with his Livy; Dio, 150 years on, fills the same hours with giants and a theatre audience; at Herculaneum the library is entombed without a word about the day. One eyewitness, one legend, one silent archive.

convergences.label: Darkness at Stabiae and Misenum
convergences.note: The same morning on opposite sides of the bay: the uncle lies on a sail on the beach at Stabiae and collapses in the fumes, while the nephew drags his mother through ash and pitch darkness away from Misenum. Neither knows the other's fate.

convergences.label: The October note and the date debate
convergences.note: A yearless charcoal scrawl, Pliny's manuscript '24 August' and Dio's seasonal phrase are the three texts every argument about the eruption's date turns on. Each was written for some other purpose; none was meant as a timestamp for the disaster.

convergences.label: Swearing by the emperor's genius, from Caligula to Vespasian
convergences.note: Thirty-five years apart, a Puteoli grain dealer (39) and a Herculaneum freedman (74–75) bind themselves with oaths by the guardian spirit of the reigning emperor — the same legal habit at either end of the bay, both preserved only by the ash.

ties.note: Nephew and adopted son. The younger Pliny inherited his uncle's name and estate, and wrote Letter 6.16 expressly to fix his uncle's heroic death in Tacitus's history.
Suetonius was Pliny's younger friend and protégé; Pliny wrote him letters and obtained privileges for him from Trajan. Both wrote about the reign in which the eruption fell.
Seneca names Pompeii, Iucundus's town, as the place worst hit by the quake; the Iucundus household's lararium relief shows the destruction Seneca describes.
A graffito by Iucundus's son Quintus supports Ceius Secundus, a man whose candidacy also appears in the painted election notices.
The October charcoal note became the leading witness against the August date in Pliny's manuscripts — opposite sides of the eruption's most famous dispute.
Pliny's naturalist uncle watched the cloud as a phenomenon to be studied; Dio's account is full of portents and giants. The two traditions — observation and omen — sit side by side in the record.

threads_out.note: Volcanologists call the most violent explosive eruptions 'Plinian' after Pliny's description of the umbrella-pine column in Letter 6.16; Krakatoa in 1883 is a classic Plinian eruption, and its far-travelling ash echoes Dio's claim that Vesuvius's dust reached Africa and Egypt.

Tambora's 1815 eruption was a Plinian eruption on a far larger scale than Vesuvius; both buried towns and their people under pyroclastic flows, preserving settlements as time capsules for later archaeologists.

Seneca's Natural Questions, written after the Campanian quake of 62/63, was the classical starting point for thinking about earthquakes and fear; Lisbon in 1755 reopened the same question of whether disaster has a moral meaning. The Herculaneum papyri were dug up in 1752–54, the same Enlightenment years.

The Wadi al-Jarf papyri of Merer and the carbonised rolls of the Villa of the Papyri are among the very few ancient papyrus finds outside Egypt's dry sands or rescued by catastrophe — one a working logbook, the other a philosopher's library.

The Babylonian astronomical diarists logged prices, weather and portents day by day; Cassius Dio's giants on Vesuvius and Pliny's careful note of the hour of the cloud show the same two impulses — omen and observation — in Roman writing about disaster.
